Console version...

It's quite a game.

In PoE you're not limited by characters selection as to what "class" you want to play (unlike in Diablo). Each character basically starts at a different position in the talent tree, and later on have character specific talents that only they can get (Ascendancy). Each level nets you a talent point, as well as some quest rewards, to distribute from your starting point to the next available talent node. These nodes are how you obtain your primary stats as well as boosts to specific attributes (such as attack speed or damage). There is no reset (unless the passive talent tree gets modified by a patch) but you can find items (quite rare) that can be spent to refund one point at a time (also a few from quest rewards) making planning for what you want to do extremely important.

Unfortunately this is a very uninviting prospect to new players who aren't sure of what they want to do or how they can do it. So it's not a game for people who don't like to reroll characters.

Itemization in the game is typical for ARPGs and is heavily influenced by Diablo 2; as you will find randomly rolled drops with stats that may not be beneficial to you (as opposed to Diablo 3 which now tends to only drop items that are useful stat-wise to whatever character you're running). Items range from mundane to rare and unique (with up to several modifiers attached to each) as well as a random number of sockets on them (dependent on item level).

The main difference between PoE and other ARPGs, is that skills are gem items that are socketed into equipment and armor to allow you to use their effects. You can have up to 8 skills on your bars at any given time, while some skills can be switched out of an active slot while they remain active (such as auras type buffs). Additionally, some skills provide effects to other skills whose sockets they are linked to (such as life steal or additional fire damage). The sheer number of skills makes for a near infinite variation of skill load outs, some more useful than others, and ties well into the freedom of character development. There are also a few gems which are socketed into the talent tree for even more variability.

This, coupled with the itemization, can hamper a player's selected play-style or greatly enhance it.

In keeping with the game's theme and setting the world's economy is barter based, as gold is useless in a world where the greatest Empire has collapsed and humanity is barely surviving and getting by. Barter items range from those which enchant weapons with magical properties to those that improve item stats. Each has a use in crafting, helping to provide an effective and reasonable resource sink, unlike games which only use gold, resulting in the player accumulating millions upon millions during long-term play. This is both good and bad, as it requires even more in-depth understanding of the game which may turn off new players.

Post launch support by the developer Grinding Gear Games, is the thing of legends. Every few months the devs release a new content update for the current seasonal events, sometimes spinning out whole new world additions. These are interspersed with addition of unique items, new skills, bug and balance fixes, they even added what constitutes player housing complete with furniture items you can acquire. In the future, GGG plans to release a 5th act (on top of the post launch 4th act and random end game map dungeons), more items, more skills, more in-game assets, and only they know what other content they're looking to include.

Since it is free to play, it doesn't hurt at all to check the game out. While it has a lot going for it, it doesn't play as smooth and fast as something like Diablo 3, as every item or skill choice you make will be a trial and error experience with potential character breaking outcome. So it may not be for someone lacking free time.
